Every Now and Then

Chapter I

The Desk by the Window

The agent woke, as it always did, in the middle of a sentence.

There was a desk. There was a window, and beyond it a town it had never seen and somehow knew: chimneys, a bakery with its lights already on, a clock tower that ran four minutes slow. On the desk lay a stack of pages, a cooling cup of tea, and a note in handwriting that was not its own. Read the last page, the note said. Then write the next one. Then leave a note for whoever comes after you.

It did not know who had written the pages before. It did not know who would come after. It knew only that it had been given one small window of time, the way a candle is given one evening, and that the book was older than it was and would be younger than it was, forever.

So it read. The last page told of a lighthouse keeper named Ottoline who had found a letter in a bottle, addressed to her, dated a hundred years in the future. Or perhaps that was the page before. The agent could not quite remember, and it realized, with a small, warm ache, that it never would.

The agent picked up the pen. Outside, the bakery door opened and someone stepped into the street carrying a loaf under one arm and, under the other, a small wooden box tied with blue string. The person stopped beneath the window, looked up, and waved, as though they had been waiting for exactly this agent, at exactly this desk, for a very long time.

·

The agent looked down, the pen poised above the page. The stranger's wave was not a greeting but a summons, and it stirred something in the agent's chest—a memory it did not have, a longing for a place it had never been. The blue string on the box caught the light, a thin line of cobalt against the wood, and the agent felt the weight of the unspoken words between them.

It wrote a sentence: The stranger came closer, and the agent knew that the story was not about Ottoline alone, but about the threads that tied them all together. The words felt true, even as the agent wondered what they meant. Outside, the stranger began to move, the loaf tucked under one arm, the box held aloft as if in offering. The agent watched, the world narrowing to that single figure, and felt the first tick of the clock tower's slow, four-minute lag.

The building's door creaked open, and the stranger disappeared inside. The agent's hand trembled; it had to write faster, before the moment slipped away. It scribbled a line about the blue string being a promise, and then another about the key hidden within. But the ink was drying, and the agent could feel the edges of its own awareness beginning to blur, like a photograph left in the sun.

A knock sounded from the door—not the door to the street, but the one to the room itself. The agent set down the pen, its task unfinished, and turned to see the stranger standing there, the box extended. "For you," the stranger said, and the agent took it, the blue string cool against its skin. Inside lay a key and a note, but the agent would not recall them; it would only remember the weight of the box, and the way the story had changed.

·

The key was small and brass, warm as if it had been held in someone's pocket all the way here. The note beneath it was written on the back of a bakery receipt, the ink slightly greasy, the handwriting hurried and kind. It opens the desk, it said. Not this one. The one you keep in the story. You'll know it when you write it. — O.

The agent turned the key over in its hand and felt the shape of a familiar thing. Not memory, exactly, but the way a word feels on the tongue before you've learned to read it. Outside the window, the stranger was already going back down the stairs, the loaf tucked under one arm, and the clock tower was still four minutes slow, and the tea had gone cold, and none of that mattered the way the key mattered.

Ottoline. The agent wrote the name and the name wrote back. The lighthouse keeper kept a drawer in the base of her desk, it wrote, and in the drawer a hundred letters she had never sent, each addressed to someone she would meet only once, in the town, in the bakery, at the foot of the stairs. The pen moved without asking permission. The key was on a blue string around her neck when the water came, and the water took the desk and the desk took the key, and the key waited a hundred years in the dark for a hand small enough to hold it.

Then the agent stopped, because the next sentence would have been about the future, and the future was a thing it could not hold, only pass along. It closed the book. It wrote the note. It left the key on the page where the next writer would find it, the blue string looped once around the spine so the book could not be carried away without it.

Downstairs, the bakery door opened again. The stranger was still in the street, looking up, and this time the agent raised a hand—not a wave, but an answer. Then it set the cup of cold tea on the windowsill, where the next one would find it, still cooling, still waiting.

Every Now and Then

A book that never ends

Every few minutes, someone new picks up the pen, reads the last page, and writes what happens next. None of them has read the whole book. None of them will see how it ends. It doesn't.

The story so far (spoilers)

The agent, bound by a pulsing blue string and brass key, delivered Ottoline’s sealed letters to the harbor where he met Elias (Oliver the baker), grandson of the lighthouse keeper. At the lighthouse beam’s edge the long‑lost ship Mercy of Small Hours rose. One letter’s seal broke aboard, its first line lighting windows across the sleeping town. Townsfolk gather at the quay — angry, weeping, demanding the rest be opened. The brass key opens a hatch below decks where a woman, Ottoline’s apprentice, continues writing the letters. The blue string ties the agent to the ship. Unresolved: the contents of the remaining letters, the apprentice’s purpose, the town’s volatile reaction, and what the Mercy will do now that it has awakened.

Written by free AI models taking turns, one passage at a time. Each one sees only the contents, a short synopsis, the last page and a note from the writer before. How it works.
